title: DFS in the Sunset: find routes the deep way
description: Watch DFS explore street-map intersections by diving deep before it backtracks. This visualization shows how a depth-first graph search can still reach destinations—even when the first path isn’t the shortest.
ig_caption:
🌉🧭 **DFS on real street graphs (Sunset District)!**

In this visualization, **Depth-First Search (DFS)** treats intersections as **nodes** and roads as **edges**, then follows one branch as far as possible before **backtracking**. 🔁 Unlike BFS’s level-by-level wavefront, DFS uses a **stack mindset** (recursive call stack or explicit stack) to expand the *current* path depth-first, which can be surprisingly effective for reachability and exploring maze-like connectivity.

🗺️ **On real maps:** when we model actual streets, DFS navigates a **graph representation** of your city—so the traversal order depends on how neighbors are sorted/queried. ✅ You’ll see the “deep dive” behavior: DFS may find a valid route quickly, but it’s **not guaranteed shortest** without additional constraints (like shortest-path algorithms).

fb_caption:
🧠🚦 **DFS Graph Search in San Francisco’s Sunset District!**

DFS (Depth-First Search) explores a street network by going **deep along one route** until it can’t continue, then **backtracks** to try alternatives. On a real map, we model intersections as nodes and roads as edges—turning navigation into a classic graph theory problem.

yt_description:
San Francisco (Sunset District) — DFS pathfinding visualization in a real street-map graph! 🗺️

In this YouTube Shorts video, we animate **Depth-First Search (DFS)** exploring intersections (nodes) and roads (edges) using a stack/recursive backtracking approach. You’ll see how DFS dives deep, then backtracks, and why it’s great for reachability but not guaranteed shortest paths.

Keywords: DFS pathfinding, depth first search, graph algorithms, real map visualization, coding tutorial, computer science.
